This relatively short gestation is complemented by a rapid developmental schedule; for example, the time since birth at weaning is 21 days [tx = 21 days] at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. The combination of small neonatal size and swift gestation suggests an energetic strategy focused on high fecundity rather than extended investment per offspring.

Puberty is attained at 60 days after birth [tp = 60 days after birth], a developmental milestone that allows individuals to potentially breed within the same season they are born at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. Field studies suggest that the combination of early weaning and early puberty permits multiple overlapping generations within a single favorable breeding season, a demographic strategy that may buffer populations against periods of poor resource availability.

Longevity records for the Algerian mouse indicate a maximum lifespan of 442 days [am = 442 days] when individuals are maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This lifespan, equivalent to approximately 14 to 15 months, is relatively brief compared to larger murids but consistent with the high mortality rates and rapid life-history pace observed in small-bodied Mediterranean rodents.
